f.title: Run risk management as a continuous lifecycle process
f.statement: Risk management is an iterative process of (1) assessing a product's benefit-risk balance, (2) developing and implementing tools to minimize its risks while preserving its benefits, (3) evaluating tool effectiveness and reassessing the benefit-risk balance, and (4) making adjustments, as appropriate, to the risk minimization tools; this four-part process should be continuous throughout a product's lifecycle, with the results of risk assessment informing the sponsor's decisions regarding risk minimization.
f.clause: II.B. Overview of the Risk Management Guidances

rows.quote:
Specifically, risk management is
an iterative process of (1) assessing a product’s benefit-risk balance, (2) developing and
implementing tools to minimize its risks while preserving its benefits, (3) evaluating tool
effectiveness and reassessing the benefit-risk balance, and (4) making adjustments, as
appropriate, to the risk minimization tools to further improve the benefit-risk balance. This four-
part process should be continuous throughout a product’s lifecycle, with the results of risk
assessment informing the sponsor’s decisions regarding risk minimization.
rows.location: II.B. Overview of the Risk Management Guidances
rows.review_note: Review: quote was cut at the line-end hyphen ('part process'); re-cut to start at 'Specifically, risk management is' keeping 'four-\npart' verbatim, so the four steps in the statement are now in the quote. f.title: Look for features suggesting a causal relationship in case reports
f.statement: In assessing case reports, sponsors should look for features that may suggest a causal relationship between product use and the adverse event, including occurrence in the expected time, absence of symptoms prior to exposure, positive dechallenge or rechallenge, consistency with established pharmacological/toxicological effects (or, for vaccines, infectious or immunologic mechanisms of injury), and consistency with known effects of other products in the class (the list continues in FDA-GVP-2005-0023).
f.clause: IV.C. Developing a Case Series

rows.quote: In assessing case reports, FDA recommends that sponsors look for features that may suggest a causal relationship between the use of a product and the adverse event, including: 1. Occurrence of the adverse event in the expected time (e.g., type 1 allergic reactions occurring within days of therapy, cancers developing after years of therapy); 2. Absence of symptoms related to the event prior to exposure; 3. Evidence of positive dechallenge or positive rechallenge; 4. Consistency of the event with the established pharmacological/toxicological effects of the product, or for vaccines, consistency with established infectious or immunologic mechanisms of injury; 5. Consistency of the event with the known effects of other products in the class;

f.title: Consider a pharmacovigilance plan when unusual safety risks become evident
f.statement: For most products routine pharmacovigilance (compliance with applicable postmarket requirements under the FDCA and FDA regulations) is sufficient for postmarketing risk assessment; in certain limited instances, unusual safety risks evident before approval or after marketing could suggest that the sponsor's consideration of a pharmacovigilance plan may be appropriate.

f.title: A pharmacovigilance plan may be developed at launch or when a risk is identified
f.statement: The development of pharmacovigilance plans may be useful at the time of product launch or when a safety risk is identified during product marketing.

f.title: Base the decision to develop a pharmacovigilance plan on scientific and logistical factors
f.statement: A sponsor's decision to develop a pharmacovigilance plan should be based on scientific and logistical factors, including the likelihood that the adverse event represents a potential safety risk, the frequency of the event, its severity, the nature of the population(s) at risk, the range of patients for which the product is indicated, and the method by which the product is dispensed (through pharmacies or performance linked systems only).
f.clause: VII. Beyond Routine Pharmacovigilance: Developing a Pharmacovigilance Plan
f.processes: Risk management & minimisation; Epidemiology / safety studies

rows.quote: FDA recommends that a sponsor’s decision to develop a pharmacovigilance plan be based on scientific and logistical factors, including the following: 1. The likelihood that the adverse event represents a potential safety risk; 2. The frequency with which the event occurs (e.g., incidence rate, reporting rate, or other measures available); 3. The severity of the event; 4. The nature of the population(s) at risk; 5. The range of patients for which the product is indicated (broad range or selected populations only); and 6. The method by which the product is dispensed (through pharmacies or performance linked systems only).
rows.location: VII. Beyond Routine Pharmacovigilance: Developing a Pharmacovigilance Plan
rows.review_note: Review: no change. Double-check: Quote proves modal, actor and all six factors.

f.title: A pharmacovigilance plan may stand alone or form part of a RiskMAP
f.statement: A pharmacovigilance plan may be developed by itself or as part of a Risk Minimization Action Plan (RiskMAP).
f.clause: VII. Beyond Routine Pharmacovigilance: Developing a Pharmacovigilance Plan

rows.quote: A pharmacovigilance plan may be developed by itself or as part of a Risk Minimization Action Plan (RiskMAP), as described in the RiskMAP Guidance.

f.statement: Sponsors may meet with representatives from the appropriate Office of New Drugs review division and the Office of Drug Safety in CDER, or the appropriate Product Office and the Division of Epidemiology, Office of Biostatistics and Epidemiology in CBER, regarding the specifics of a given product's pharmacovigilance plan.

f.title: Use a pharmacovigilance plan for products with serious risks or unstudied at-risk populations
f.statement: For a product without safety risks identified pre- or post-approval and with adequately studied at-risk populations, routine spontaneous reporting will be sufficient; pharmacovigilance plans may be appropriate for products for which serious safety risks have been identified pre- or post-approval, or at-risk populations have not been adequately studied.
f.clause: VII. Beyond Routine Pharmacovigilance: Developing a Pharmacovigilance Plan

rows.quote: FDA believes that for a product without safety risks identified pre- or post-approval and for which at-risk populations are thought to have been adequately studied, routine spontaneous reporting will be sufficient for postmarketing surveillance. On the other hand, pharmacovigilance plans may be appropriate for products for which: (1) serious safety risks have been identified pre- or post-approval, or (2) at-risk populations have not been adequately studied.

rows.review_note: Review: no change. Double-check: "FDA believes ... may be appropriate" is descriptive; Permitted and actor are judgement calls.

f.title: Sponsors may discuss with FDA whether a pharmacovigilance plan is appropriate
f.statement: Sponsors may discuss with the Agency the nature of the safety concerns posed by such a product and the determination whether a pharmacovigilance plan is appropriate.

f.title: Consider enhanced reporting and active surveillance elements in a pharmacovigilance plan
f.statement: A pharmacovigilance plan could include: submission of specific serious adverse event reports in an expedited manner beyond routine required reporting (i.e., as 15-day reports); submission of adverse event report summaries at more frequent, prespecified intervals (e.g., quarterly rather than annually); and active surveillance to identify adverse events that may or may not be reported through passive surveillance, which can be drug based, setting based (e.g., emergency departments) or event based (e.g., acute liver failure).
f.clause: VII. Beyond Routine Pharmacovigilance: Developing a Pharmacovigilance Plan
f.processes: Risk management & minimisation; Epidemiology / safety studies

rows.quote: A pharmacovigilance plan could include one or more of the following elements: 1. Submission of specific serious adverse event reports in an expedited manner beyond routine required reporting (i.e., as 15-day reports); 2. Submission of adverse event report summaries at more frequent, prespecified intervals (e.g., quarterly rather than annually); 3. Active surveillance to identify adverse events that may or may not be reported through passive surveillance. Active surveillance can be (1) drug based: identifying adverse events in patients taking certain products, (2) setting based: identifying adverse events in certain health care settings where they are likely to present for treatment (e.g., emergency departments, etc.), or (3) event based: identifying adverse events that are likely to be associated with medical products (e.g., acute liver failure);
rows.location: VII. Beyond Routine Pharmacovigilance: Developing a Pharmacovigilance Plan
rows.review_note: Review: no change (items 1-3; items 4-6 in FDA-GVP-2005-0085). Permitted confirmed ('could include'). Deadline records the 15-day/periodic elements only as options of a plan. Double-check: "could include" read as Permitted; actor inferred. Deadline cleared: the 15-day and periodic intervals are optional plan elements, not deadlines of this row.

f.title: Consider additional studies, registries, surveys or trials in a pharmacovigilance plan
f.statement: A pharmacovigilance plan could also include additional pharmacoepidemiologic studies (e.g., in automated claims or other databases) using cohort, case-control or other appropriate designs; creation of registries or implementation of patient or health care provider surveys; and additional controlled clinical trials.

f.title: Re-evaluate the safety risk and pharmacovigilance plan effectiveness as data emerge
f.statement: As data emerge, a sponsor should re-evaluate the safety risk and the effectiveness of its pharmacovigilance plan, which may result in revisions to the plan.

f.title: Sponsors may take interim risk communication actions with FDA
f.statement: While additional information is being developed, sponsors working with FDA can take interim actions to communicate information about potential safety risks (e.g., through labeling) to minimize the risk to users of the product.
